problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###  

**a. Verdict**  
I have found a complete solution. The minimum possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Permutation‑matrix viewpoint** –  
   The uncovered unit squares must form a set containing exactly one square in each row and each column; therefore they are the entries of a permutation matrix.  
   Let \(\pi\) be the permutation on \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (\(n=2025\)) such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,\pi(i))\).

2. **Decomposition of the board** –  
   Define  

   \[
   L=\{(i,j):j<\pi(i)\},\qquad   
   R=\{(i,j):j>\pi(i)\}.
   \]

   \(L\) (cells left of the holes) and \(R\) (cells right of the holes) are disjoint and together contain all covered cells.

3. **Upper bound (construction)** –  
   Choose the identity permutation \(\pi(i)=i\).  
   * Left part \(L\) (below the main diagonal) is tiled by the vertical rectangles  

     \[
     T_c=\{(i,c):i=c+1,\dots ,n\},\qquad c=1,\dots ,n-1 .
     \]

   * Right part \(R\) (above the main diagonal) is tiled by the horizontal rectangles  

     \[
     H_r=\{(r,j):j=r+1,\dots ,n\},\qquad r=1,\dots ,n-1 .
     \]

   These are \( (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) pairwise‑disjoint rectangles, showing  

   \[
   \text{minimum}\le 2n-2 .
   \]

4. **Lower bound – counting “runs’’**  

   *For the left part.*  
   Fix a column \(c\;(1\le c\le n-1)\).  
   The rows that contain a cell of \(L\) in column \(c\) are exactly  

   \[
   S_c=\{\,i\mid \pi(i)>c\,\}.
   \]

   Write the binary sequence \(f_c(i)=\mathbf 1_{\{\pi(i)>c\}}\) for \(i=1,\dots ,n\).  
   The set \(S_c\) splits into a collection of **maximal consecutive blocks** (runs of 1’s); denote the number of such runs by \(b_c\).  
   A rectangle intersecting column \(c\) must be contained in a single run, otherwise it would have to cover a row where column \(c\) is absent – which would contain the uncovered square of that row, contradicting the rules.  
   Hence at least \(b_c\) distinct rectangles are needed to cover the cells of column \(c\) in \(L\). Summing over all columns,

   \[
   \#\text{rectangles covering }L\;\ge\;\sum_{c=1}^{n-1} b_c .\tag{1}
   \]

   **Lemma 1.** \(\displaystyle\sum_{c=1}^{n-1} b_c \ge n-1\).

   *Proof.*  
   Scan the rows from \(i=1\) to \(i=n\). For each adjacent pair \((i,i+1)\) consider the change \(\Delta_i=|\pi(i+1)-\pi(i)|\).  
   If \(\pi(i+1)>\pi(i)\), then for every column \(c\) with \(\pi(i)<c\le\pi(i+1)\) the binary sequence \(f_c\) switches from 0 at row \(i\) to 1 at row \(i+1\); this creates a **new run** of 1’s in column \(c\).  
   If \(\pi(i+1)<\pi(i)\), then for every column \(c\) with \(\pi(i+1)<c\le\pi(i)\) the sequence switches from 1 to 0, ending a run and simultaneously starting a new run at the next row. In both cases exactly \(|\pi(i+1)-\pi(i)|\) new runs appear across the columns.  

   Therefore  

   \[
   \sum_{c=1}^{n-1} b_c
   =\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} |\pi(i+1)-\pi(i)|.
   \]

   The right‑hand sum is minimized when the permutation is monotone increasing, i.e. \(\pi(i)=i\), giving \(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}1=n-1\). For any other permutation at least one difference exceeds 1, so the sum is \(\ge n-1\). ∎

   Combining (1) with Lemma 1 yields  

   \[
   \#\text{rectangles covering }L\;\ge\;n-1 .
   \tag{2}
   \]

   *For the right part.*  
   Apply the same argument to the reflected board (replace column \(j\) by \(n+1-j\)). The right part \(R\) also needs at least \(n-1\) rectangles.  

   Consequently any admissible tiling uses at least  

   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
   \]

   rectangles. This is the lower bound (3).

5. **Conclusion** –  
   The construction of step 3 uses exactly \(2n-2\) rectangles, and the lower bound (3) shows that fewer are impossible. Hence the minimum number of tiles is precisely \(2n-2\).  

   For the original board \(n=2025\),

   \[
   \boxed{2\cdot2025-2 = 4048}.
   \]

   An explicit tiling attaining the bound is described in the construction: uncovered squares on the main diagonal, vertical strips below it, and horizontal strips above it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**### Detailed Solution ###**

Let \(n=2025\).  
A placement of axis‑parallel rectangular tiles in which each row and each column contains exactly one uncovered unit square forces the set of uncovered squares to be a **permutation matrix**: there exists a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is the cell \((i,\pi(i))\).

Define  

\[
L=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le n,\;j<\pi(i)\},\qquad   
R=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le n,\;j>\pi(i)\}.
\]

\(L\) consists of all cells strictly to the left of the uncovered squares, \(R\) those strictly to the right.  The two sets are disjoint and together contain every covered cell.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1. Upper bound – an explicit tiling

Choose the identity permutation \(\pi(i)=i\) (the uncovered squares are the main diagonal cells \((i,i)\)).

*Left part.*  
For each column \(c\) with \(1\le c\le n-1\) let  

\[
T_c=\{(i,c)\mid i=c+1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

\(T_c\) is a vertical rectangle of size \((n-c)\times1\).  
The family \(\{T_c\}_{c=1}^{n-1}\) covers exactly the cells of \(L\) and the rectangles are pairwise disjoint.

*Right part.*  
For each row \(r\) with \(1\le r\le n-1\) let  

\[
H_r=\{(r,j)\mid j=r+1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

\(H_r\) is a horizontal rectangle of size \(1\times (n-r)\).  
The family \(\{H_r\}_{r=1}^{n-1}\) covers exactly the cells of \(R\) and the rectangles are pairwise disjoint.

Thus the whole board (except the diagonal holes) is tiled with  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
\]

rectangles. Consequently  

\[
\text{minimum number of tiles}\le 2n-2 .
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2. Lower bound – any tiling needs at least \(2n-2\) rectangles

Fix an arbitrary admissible tiling and the associated permutation \(\pi\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Lemma 1.** The left part \(L\) requires at least \(n-1\) rectangles.

*Proof.*  
For a fixed column \(c\;(1\le c\le n-1)\) consider the binary sequence  

\[
f_c(i)=\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if }\pi(i)>c,\\[2pt]
0,&\text{if }\pi(i)\le c,
\end{cases}\qquad i=1,\dots ,n .
\]

The rows that contain a cell of \(L\) in column \(c\) are precisely those with \(f_c(i)=1\).  
Write these rows as a union of maximal consecutive blocks (runs of 1’s); let the number of such runs be \(b_c\).

A rectangle intersecting column \(c\) must be contained wholly inside a single run, because if it spanned two distinct runs it would have to include a row where column \(c\) is absent – that row contains the uncovered square of its column, which a tile may not cover. Hence at least \(b_c\) distinct rectangles are needed to cover the cells of column \(c\) in \(L\).

Summing over all columns gives  

\[
\#\text{rectangles covering }L\;\ge\;\sum_{c=1}^{n-1} b_c .\tag{5}
\]

Now examine how the runs appear when we move from row \(i\) to row \(i+1\).  
If \(\pi(i+1)>\pi(i)\) then for each column \(c\) with \(\pi(i)<c\le\pi(i+1)\) the value of \(f_c\) changes from \(0\) at row \(i\) to \(1\) at row \(i+1\); this creates a new run of 1’s in column \(c\).  
If \(\pi(i+1)<\pi(i)\) then for each column \(c\) with \(\pi(i+1)<c\le\pi(i)\) the value of \(f_c\) changes from \(1\) to \(0\); the run of 1’s that ended at row \(i\) is followed by a new run (starting at row \(i+1\)). In both cases exactly \(|\pi(i+1)-\pi(i)|\) new runs appear across the columns.

Therefore  

\[
\sum_{c=1}^{n-1} b_c
   =\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} |\pi(i+1)-\pi(i)|.
\tag{6}
\]

The right‑hand sum is minimized when the permutation is monotone increasing, i.e. \(\pi(i)=i\), giving \(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}1=n-1\). For any other permutation at least one difference exceeds \(1\), so the sum is \(\ge n-1\). Consequently  

\[
\sum_{c=1}^{n-1} b_c \ge n-1 .
\]

Together with (5) this yields the desired bound \(\#\text{rectangles covering }L\ge n-1\). ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Lemma 2.** The right part \(R\) also requires at least \(n-1\) rectangles.

*Proof.*  
Reflect the board horizontally (replace column \(j\) by column \(n+1-j\)). Under this reflection the right part \(R\) becomes a left part of the reflected board, to which Lemma 1 applies. Hence the same lower bound holds for \(R\). ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Adding the two lemmas we obtain  

\[
\text{any admissible tiling uses at least }(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\text{ rectangles}. \tag{7}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3. Completion of the proof

From the explicit construction (4) we have a tiling with exactly \(2n-2\) rectangles, and from (7) no tiling can use fewer. Therefore the minimum possible number of tiles is precisely  

\[
2n-2.
\]

For the original problem \(n=2025\),

\[
\boxed{2\cdot2025-2 = 4048}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Explicit example for the \(2025\times2025\) board**

* Uncovered squares: the main diagonal cells \((i,i)\) for \(i=1,\dots ,2025\).  
* Tiles below the diagonal (vertical): for each column \(c=1,\dots ,2024\) place the rectangle  

  \[
  T_c=\{(i,c)\mid i=c+1,\dots ,2025\},
  \]

  of size \((2025-c)\times1\).

* Tiles above the diagonal (horizontal): for each row \(r=1,\dots ,2024\) place the rectangle  

  \[
  H_r=\{(r,j)\mid j=r+1,\dots ,2025\},
  \]

  of size \(1\times(2025-r)\).

These \(2024+2024=4048\) rectangles are pairwise disjoint, avoid the diagonal holes, and satisfy the requirement that each row and each column contains exactly one uncovered unit square. Hence the bound is attainable.
